title: E++ Guided Tutorial
description: The official E++ lesson pack. This file — not the IDE — is the single source of truth for tutorial content. Edit it and reload the IDE, or import your own pack from the tutorial dialog.

lessons.title: Welcome to E++ (Dev Build 6.1)
lessons.summary: E++ is an English-like language based on WeeklyHow's AI video, where AI was asked to create a coding language that reads like human language.
lessons.explanation: Statements in E++ end with a period (.) or a newline. Comments start with "note:". The word "say" prints text to the console. Press Run (or Ctrl+Enter) to try every example.
lessons.code:
note: Welcome to E++ Dev Build 6.1!
note: Based on WeeklyHow's AI programming language video.
say "Hello, world!"
say "E++ looks like English, reads like English, and behaves like code."

lessons.title: Variables & Quotes
lessons.summary: Define variables with "Define <name> as <value>." Variables are ALWAYS referenced inside single quotes ('name').
lessons.explanation: Text in double quotes is literal. Single quotes refer to a variable you defined earlier. Join pieces of text with the word "plus".
lessons.code:
Define name as WeeklyHow.
say "Hello " plus 'name' plus "!"
Define score as 100.
say "Your starting score is " plus 'score'
set 'score' to 125
say "Your score is now " plus 'score' plus "."

lessons.title: English Maths
lessons.summary: Maths uses plain English words like plus, minus and times. Change number variables with Increase and Decrease.
lessons.explanation: Precedence works naturally: parentheses first, then times, then plus and minus. Increase and Decrease change a number variable in place.
lessons.code:
say 10 plus 5 times 2
say (10 plus 5) times 2

Define counter as 10.
Increase counter by 5
say "Counter after increase: " plus 'counter'
Decrease counter by 3
say "Counter after decrease: " plus 'counter'

lessons.title: Questions & Conditions
lessons.summary: Ask questions with "ask ... and save answer as <name>", then test the answer with natural-sounding "if" statements.
lessons.explanation: Answers from ask arrive as text, but E++ compares them numerically when it makes sense. Use "otherwise" for the other branch, and "contains" to look inside text.
lessons.code:
ask "What is 5 plus 6?" and save answer as answer
if 'answer' is equal to 11 then
  say "Spot on! That is correct."
otherwise
  say "Not quite — the answer was 11."
end if

Define sentence as "The quick brown fox"
if 'sentence' contains "fox" then say "Found a fox!"

lessons.title: Loops & Changing Values
lessons.summary: Repeat work with "repeat N times ... end repeat", and let values change as the loop runs.
lessons.explanation: A loop runs the lines between "repeat" and "end repeat". Try changing the number of repeats, and watch the counter fall.
lessons.code:
Define count as 3.

repeat 3 times
  say 'count'
  Set count to 'count' minus 1.
end repeat

say "Blast off!"

lessons.title: .eppl vs .eppla
lessons.summary: A .eppl file is strictly E++ without libraries. A .eppla file unlocks every library.
lessons.explanation: Keeping pure code in .eppl means it runs anywhere — including inside the standalone E++.zip runtime. The moment a program needs a library such as Math, Text, Random, Draw, Image or Python, it belongs in a .eppla file.
lessons.code:
note: This lesson uses a library, so its tutorial file is .eppla.
note: Pure code that avoids libraries stays .eppl.
add library "Math"

say square root of 81
say 1 divided by 2 as decimal
say "Five plus five is " plus (5 plus 5)

lessons.title: Libraries: Math, Text & Random
lessons.summary: Add a library with "add library \"Name\"" and new words become part of the language.
lessons.explanation: Libraries extend E++ with extra English verbs. Math adds fractions, decimals, roots and powers. Text works on words and sentences. Random invents numbers for you.
lessons.code:
note: Save this as a .eppla file to use libraries.
add library "Math"
add library "Text"
add library "Random"

display 1 divided by 2 as fraction
say uppercase of "hello e++"
say length of "How long am I?"
say "A random number: " plus (random number between 1 and 10)

lessons.title: Python Inside E++
lessons.summary: The Python library lets real Python run from inside an E++ program, using commas ", ... ," for multi-line blocks.
lessons.explanation: Python errors are reported with Python's own error names, so what you learn here transfers straight to Python. Multi-line Python uses a comma at the start and end instead of dashes.
lessons.code:
add library "Python"

python code "print('Hello from Python inside E++!')"

python code ",for number in range(3):
    print('Python count:', number)
,"

say "Back to plain English in E++!"

lessons.title: Images from Base64 Text
lessons.summary: The Image library turns Base64 text into a picture you can show in the console.
lessons.explanation: Base64 is a way of writing any file as plain text. The Image library auto-detects PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP, so you only need "define", "check if ... exists" and "display image".
lessons.code:
note: The Image library is new in Dev Build 5 and works in .eppla files.
add library "Image"

define 'red pixel' as image "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mP8/5+hHgAHggJ/PchI7wAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="

check if 'red pixel' exists
display image 'red pixel'

check if 'missing picture' exists
say "If the first image appeared above, the Image library works!"

lessons.title: Drawing Sprites
lessons.summary: The Draw library puts a sprite in the middle of a canvas and moves it around with plain English.
lessons.explanation: Sprites start at (0, 0), the centre of the drawing panel. Pixel amounts are always written as text in double quotes, like "60".
lessons.code:
define 'hero' as drawing sprite
'hero' move right "60"
'hero' move down "30"
'hero' move left "20"
'hero' move up "10"

say "The hero sprite has moved — look at the drawing panel."
